If consideration of PPM 90-2 Land Use Category "E" for interior L10 traffic generated design year noise levels is applied to the residential structures, taking into account a noise (dBA) reduction factor from the predicted exterior L10 traffic generated noise level, based on the aforementioned assumption and the existing and/or anticipated future structural condition of the buildings, the traffic generated design year 1990 predicted interior L10 noise levels range from 38.2 dBA to 60.9 dBA. Of the twenty-eight (28) sites designated Land Use Category "B/E", the predicted interior traffic generated design year L10 noise level for eighteen (18) sites would be less than or equal to the design year interior L10 noise level standard of 55 dBA contained in PPM 90-2.
At the present time, there is no FHWA policy concerning the amount of noise increase which would constitute a major noise impact. Generally, an increase in noise levels of 1 to 5 decibels (dBA) is not perceptually distinguishable to the human ear. It has been suggested by some informed experts that an increase of 5 to 10 decibels is minor, J0 to 15 decibels is moderate, and 15 or more decibels is significant (or severe).4,5,6
The National Cooperative Highway Research Program Report 117-- Highway Noise, A Design Guide for Highway Engineers, -- states:
"Intermittent excesses due, for instance, to passing trucks should not exceed the range of ambient levels by more than 10 dBA. It is noted that extraordinary events such as very close truck passages or low aircraft flyovers may produce levels that exceed ambient levels by 25 to 35 dBA; although people may be acclimatized to such events, if they occur frequently, individual or public complaints may be precipitated. Thus, the 10 dBA excursion allowed for infrequent events by the foregoing criterion is conservative.
